En route Singapore-Batavia
Dear Family,
We are flying along the coast of Sumatra
with Batavia,
or I should say Jakarta, two hours away. The people of the
United States of Indonesia in their swing away from the Dutch
toward extreme nationalism have changed the name of world-known
Batavia to Jakarta and the U.S.I. Post Office has announced
that after April Ist all mail addressed to "Batavia" will be sent
to the dead letter office! In like manner, and about as sensible,
the Philippines are talking about the abolition of English and
Spanish in favor of Togolug - the most used of some eighty Phil-
ippine dialects.
It is as though our forebearers had abolished
English ar er the Revolution and adopted Choctaw or some other
Indian language. Ridiculous, of course, but it shows just how
far these people will go in their almost fanatical netionalism.
Singapore, in the extreme south of the Malay Peninsula
is only sixteen miles north of the equator.
It is on an island
bought by the British from the Sultan of Johore. Here the
vessels of the seven seas must pass through the narrow Straits
of Malacca, under the guns of the British who take a modest toll
from each
and every passerby.
During the war the British
Malaya to first resist Japanese invasion and then occupation.
Guns and ammunition were smuggled in all along the extensive
coastline, and many promises were made by the military com-
manders few of which were kept by the political bigwigs after
the war was won.
As a result there grew up in Malaya the
"Peoples Anti-British Army" which is
a motley collection of
patriots, communists and bandits which has terrorized the entire
peninsula and paralyzed business especially the large rubber
plantations.
Apparently the leaders are determined to make life
so tough for their white masters that none will wish to stay.
Nothing short of a major military operation can succeed against
them.
That would be costiy both in money and lives, but the
British have no choice but to clean up the entire peninsula or
get out, and I can't understand why the Labor Government con-
tinues to temporize and take less than the obviously required
measures. One thing sure, if "Winnie" gets back in control he
will soon put an end to the open season on Englishmen.
He will
go part way back to the good old buccaneering days of Victoria,
the East India Company and Raffles of Singapore.

En route Jakarta-Singapore
March Il, 1950
You have a feeling in this part of the world that you
are living on top of a volcano or at least near one.
quiet, the countryside is beautiful and the people outwardly
friendly, but the volcano may erupt at any moment. Most of the
revolutionists are young men who - as in the case of the bright
young C.C.N.Y. "do gooders" who flocked to F.D.R. and the New
Deal - are concerned only with the creation of
a bright new
world. None of them has ever met a payroll. We have had the
New Deal, then the Fair Deal and now - as someone put it - the
The Indonesians are having plenty of the latter.
fortunately for the young, starry-eyed leaders the Chinese,
who have most of the money in Malaya, Singapre end the U.S.I.,
will not conform to the new, or for that matter to any other,
rules. So the new governments of the Philippines and Indonesia
write regulations which are a constant source of grief and
anguish to the Americans, British and Dutch businessmen but
bother the Chinese not at all.
Furthermore, the Chinese are so
much smarter than any of the other people that they inevitably
find a way not only to get around the regulations but to make
money out of the confusion caused by said regulations in the
conforming competitive foreign firms.
Arriving at Batavia we found that our cable for hotel
reservations had not arrived.
The least undesirable hostelery
is the Hotel Des Indies.
Our Agents learned we were en route
from K.L.M. and so desperate is the housing problem in Batavia
that they appealed to the Americen Ambassador for help.
Ev-
entually we got a room reserved for the Shell Petroleum Com-
pany and they moved a cot in for Hebe.
We had a drink with
old friends from the Philippines, Mr. and Mrs. Calhoun, (he
is National City Bank #1 for
the
East) an early dinner and
to mosquito-net-bedecked bed.
The next morning, March 10th,
Debby and Hebe drove out some thirty-five miles
to a famous
Botanical Garden while I called on our agents MeClain, Watson
& Company, a British firm founded in 1827.
Also called on
our Ambassador to pay my respects and thank him for getting
us a room.
Debby and Hebe had Rijstaffle with Mrs. Calhoun
while I had lunch at a club with the Directors of Mclain,
Watson.
The club was the former country. home of Raffles
i pre-
sented by him to the business community of Batavia as a club
with the proviso that "food and drink shall be available at
all hours on all days".
The Ambassador, Mr. Cochran, gave me a lot of in-
formation about the Export-Import Bank loan of one hundred

-3-
million dollars to the new government, the need of hotel con-
struction and the advantages of tourism to the economy of the
U.S.I.
However, he, in common with Calhoun and our agents,
advised that we should wait a while to see what happens before
undertaking any hotel construction in Jakarta.
The city is so
full of Dutchmen from the unsafe countryside that the population
is three or four times normal. K.L.M. is doing a thriving
business westbound carrying disillusioned Dutchmen back to
Holland. The guilder official rate of exchange is slięhtly over
three to one US dollar, while the Flack Market rate is twenty-
five to one.
A new Ford car costs the equivalent of US $3,000
but can be sold for US $10,000 in the Black Merket.
We hed dinner last night with Henry and Lynn Cooper
at the Hotel Des Indies. Henry was fuming over a Coco Cola
which he had purchased for $1.00 US, so confidentielly we made
a trip to Chinatown where I converted enough Singapore Straits
dollars to pay our hotel bill, buy some sarongs (for a couple
of bucks each instead of the legal (25 each) and also pay the
Cooper brothers' expenses in Batavia and leave them a tidy sum
over for their trip to Bali.
They had declared all their cur-
rency when they
entered but I just happened to forget about my
The Dutch were somewhat concerned over the renegade
"Turk" Westerling who was arrested in Singapore while we were
there. He is a soldier of fortune who fights for principal
not principle, but he rallied a number of Dutch Army deserters
to his ranks and when, for example, he marched into Bandoeng
the Indonesian soldiers fled and the Dutch garrison looked the
The concern was because having made peace with the
U.S.I. the Dutch are worried over the possibility of anti-Dutch
sentiment which is building up in the Islands.
The natives say
that under centuries of Dutch rule no natives ever made any
money, but they ignore the fact that the Chinese under that
same rule got rich as did also the Arabs who can out-Chinese
the Chinese and out-Jew the Jews.
En route Singapore-Bangkok
Ile landed at Singapore for an hour then took off and
flew north over the viaduct
which connects the Island with the
mainland.
Then over Kota Bahru on the border between Malaya
and Siam where the Japanese first landed. Of course, just south
of Singapore we again crossed the equator. Going down to Jakarta
Hebe made her first trip "down under". Debby is en ola timer,
and I have crossed in the South Pacific, South America on botn
coasts, south Atlantic, west and east Africa.

A ROMAN GENERAL'S OPINION OF "MILITARY CRITICS"
LUCIUS AEMILIUS PAULUS, 8. Roman Consul, who had been
selected to conduct the war with the Macedonians,
B.C. 168, went out from the Senate-house into the
assembly of the people and addressed them as follows:
"In every circle, and, truly, at every table, there are perple
who lead armies into Macedonia; who know where the camp ought to
be placed; what posts ought to be occupied by troops; when and
through what pass that territory should be entered; where magazines
should be formed; how provisions should be conveyed by land and
sea; and when it is proper to engage the enemy, when to lie quiet,
And they not only determine what is best to be done, but if anything
is done in any other manner than what they have pointed out, they
arraign the consul, as if he were on trial before them. These are
great impediments to those who have the management of affairs; for
everyone cennot encounter injurious reports with the same con-
stancy and firmness and mind as Fabius did, who chose to let his
own ability be questioned through the folly of the people, rather
than to mismanage the public business with a high reputation. I
am not one of those who think that commanders ought at no time
to receive advice; on the contrary, I should deem that man more
proud than wise, who regulated every proceeding by the standard
of his own single judgement. What then is my opinion? That com-
manders should be counselled, chiefly, by persons of known talent;
by those who have made the art of war their particular study,
and whose knowledge is derived from experience; from those who
are present at the scene of action, who see
the country, who see
the enemy; who see the advantages that occasions offer, and who,
like people embarked in the same ship, are sharers of the danger.
If, therefore, anyone thinks himself qualified to give advice
respecting the war which I am to conduct, which may prove advan-
tageous to the public, let him not refuse his assistance to the
state, but let him come with me into Mecedonia.
He shall be
furnished with a ship, a horse, a tent; even his travelling
charges shall be defrayed. But if he thinks this too much trouble,
and prefers the repose of a city life to the toils of war, let
him not, on land, assume the office of a pilot.
The city, in
itself, furnishes abundance of topics for conversation; let it
confine its passion for talking within its own precincts, and
rest assured that we shall pay no attention to any councils but
such as shall be framed within our camp."
LIVY, (*TITUS LIVIUS) History of Rome.
Vol. 7, Book XLIV, Chapter 22.
Translation by Beorge Baker, A.M.
*TITUS LIVIUS (LIVY) born 59 B.C., died A.D. 17.
